strengths: Combining BORE-style optimization with label propagation and label spreading is a coherent, potentially useful contribution. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and existing candidate pools broadens its applicability, and the relationship to BORE, LFBO, and graph-based semi-supervised learning is explained.

The evaluation covers synthetic functions, four tabular hyperparameter benchmarks, three NATS-Bench datasets, and MNIST search, with ten repetitions and relevant GP, BORE, and LFBO baselines. The reported curves show promising improvements, particularly on continuous synthetic benchmarks and NATS-Bench.

The supplementary experiments examine bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. The comparison against the no-unlabeled-data estimator provides useful evidence that unlabeled points contribute to performance on the tested synthetic problems.
weaknesses: Major theoretical gap: Section 4.3 does not establish the superiority claimed below Equation (8). The cited minimax argument concerns the existence of a semi-supervised learner and comparison with an oracle possessing decision-set information; it does not establish a bound for the proposed label propagation/spreading algorithm. Applicability to adaptively collected optimization data and the connection between classification risk and optimization performance are also unproven. Moreover, sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that high-density connected regions have the same objective-threshold label.

The central overconfidence explanation remains insufficiently demonstrated. Section 3.1 defines it through concentration of high positive-class probabilities, but a small positive region can be correct, and expanding that region need not improve exploration or cover a global optimum. The qualitative Branin examples and optimization curves do not establish this mechanism. Quantitative measurements of candidate-region coverage and an ablation of random tie-breaking would strengthen the causal claim; the existing no-unlabeled-data comparison is limited to two synthetic functions.

Important reproduction details are missing or unclear: the bandwidth and clamping factor used in the main experiments, propagation stopping settings, feature scaling and categorical encoding, pool subsample sizes, and acquisition maximization over finite candidate pools. These omissions materially affect confidence in the comparisons because Figure s.4 demonstrates substantial bandwidth sensitivity. Pseudocode and a promise of future code release do not resolve these choices.

The MNIST experiment uses a representation trained on 440,000 labeled examples to predict exactly the three-digit number being minimized, achieving 96.9% test accuracy. This supplies extensive information about the optimization objective. A baseline that directly ranks candidates using the pretrained predictor is needed to establish the value of additional optimization, and this experiment provides limited evidence for optimization with scarce objective labels.

Practical scalability is insufficiently evaluated. The dense similarity graph has quadratic storage requirements, and continuous acquisition optimization uses 1,000 starts, yet no runtime or memory comparisons are reported. Subsampling experiments on small synthetic pools do not establish the tradeoff on the much larger application pools. Continuous-domain evaluation is also confined to two-dimensional functions.

Minor presentation issues include inconsistent row/column normalization conventions for the transition matrix in Section 4.1, very small plot legends, and undefined shaded uncertainty bands. Defining the plotted statistics would make close empirical comparisons easier to assess.
